method: Core commitments: statements on which every sincere adherent of an ideology must be on one side. Three Opus coders (lenses: theorist, insider, sceptic) proposed commitments independently; an entry is kept when at least 2 of 3 proposed it (coders = how many), and each was checked against the ideology's coded answer sheet (required side at |v| >= 2 in every required frame). side is the sign of the raw answer (+1 agree, -1 disagree) to the statement as worded; the item key is not applied. frame I checks the ideal-system answer; both also checks here and now. A decisive contradiction (|answer| >= 2 on the wrong side) rules the ideology out. Entries whose simulated sincere adherents are wrongly ruled out more than 2% of the time are moved to dropped by scripts/commitments-audit.ts. Entries refuted by a counterexample (sincere mainstream adherents who reject the statement on principle) are moved to dropped by hand, with the reason. Raw coder output: commitments-raw.json.

marxism-leninism.why: Social ownership of the means of production, through the state and collectives, is the economic base the doctrine is built on.
An economy where nearly all productive assets are privately owned is capitalism, which Marxism-Leninism exists to abolish.
Leninist theory has the dictatorship of the proletariat run through a single vanguard party, with rival parties banned as class enemies.

trotskyism.why: Trotskyism aims at a workers' state where the means of production are owned collectively.
Nearly universal private ownership of productive assets is the capitalism that Trotskyism sets out to overthrow.
Permanent revolution and its rejection of socialism in one country put working-class internationalism ahead of national loyalty, now as well as in the ideal.
Trotsky's programme requires a democratically planned economy, coordinated nationally and ultimately worldwide, not one run by market competition.

democratic-socialism.why: Democratic socialism, unlike social democracy, wants the major means of production owned socially by the public, by cooperatives or by workers.
An economy where nearly all productive assets are privately owned contradicts its goal of social ownership of major enterprises.
Democratic socialism treats competitive multiparty elections as part of socialism itself, which is what separates it from one-party communism.

market-socialism.why: Every model of market socialism, from Yugoslav self-management to coupon socialism, makes firms worker-owned or socially owned.
Nearly universal private ownership of productive assets would remove the 'socialism' from market socialism.
Private shareholder ownership of large firms is the capitalist ownership that market socialism replaces.
Market socialism is defined by letting markets and prices, not a central plan, decide what is produced.

eco-socialism.why: Eco-socialism takes energy, land and key industries into common ownership so production can be organised around ecological limits.
The tradition blames private capitalist ownership and its drive to grow for the ecological crisis.
Eco-socialists hold that profit-driven market allocation cannot respect planetary limits, so prices and competition alone cannot decide production.

african-socialism.why: African socialism holds land communally and puts the major means of production under peasants and workers through the state and cooperatives.
Ujamaa's founding principle is that nobody exploits and the community cares for all, so it cannot accept a large rich-poor divide.
Every variant gives national planning priorities and communal needs a role that pure price competition would rule out.

social-democracy.why: Reducing inequality through progressive taxes and universal welfare is the tradition's central purpose.
Rule by one permanent party abolishes the parliamentary democracy that social democracy depends on.
Social democracy holds that markets left alone distribute wealth unjustly and must be shaped by democratic politics.

progressive-liberalism.why: Modern progressive liberalism treats LGBTQ equality, including equal marriage, as a civil right.

green-politics.why: Grassroots democracy is one of the four Green pillars, so permanent rule by one party without rivals contradicts it.
Giving one leader power to act without elected lawmakers contradicts the participatory, grassroots democracy pillar.
Non-violence is a founding pillar, so Greens reject armed force abroad for national interests when no one has attacked.
Ecological wisdom requires keeping production within planetary limits, which unregulated price competition does not do.

left-populism.why: Its basic divide is the many against an enriched few, and it calls for redistributing that concentrated wealth.
Left populism is defined by opposing the gap between the many and a privileged oligarchy.
Left populism defines democracy as the people ruling rather than unelected technocrats, so voters must outweigh experts.
It holds that markets must not override the popular will and wants public control of key sectors.

social-liberalism.why: Social liberalism wants a mainly private, market-coordinated economy, so common ownership of nearly all assets contradicts it.

centrism.why: Centrism backs a regulated market economy, which nearly complete common ownership of productive assets would abolish.
Centrism backs liberal democracy with checks and balances, which one-party rule abolishes.
Distrust of concentrated power and support for checks and balances rule out a leader acting without lawmakers' approval.

third-way.why: Its defining move was dropping wholesale common ownership in favour of a market economy.
The Third Way works within representative democracy and seeks to modernise it, so it rejects one-party rule.
The Third Way rejects the old left's command economy and accepts markets as the main coordinator.

neoliberalism.why: Private property is a foundation of the neoliberal order, and it privatises state enterprises.
Open trade without protectionist barriers is a core neoliberal principle.
Neoliberal thought holds that prices coordinate dispersed knowledge better than any planner can.
Neoliberalism holds that capital should go to its most profitable use as markets judge it, not toward goals set by planners.

liberal-conservatism.why: Free enterprise and private property are the economic-liberal half of liberal conservatism.
Liberal conservatism defends liberal democracy and parliamentary institutions as inherited goods, and one-party rule destroys them.
Liberal conservatives hold that markets should coordinate the economy, not a central plan.

traditional-conservatism.why: Traditional conservatism treats private property as a bulwark of independence and continuity.
Burkean scepticism of grand rational planning rules out running the economy by a deliberate central plan.

paleoconservatism.why: Paleoconservatism opposes supranational bodies overriding national self-government.
Paleoconservatives rank loyalty to their own particular people above abstract universal humanity.
Paleoconservatism treats the nation as a historic people and calls for immigration to be sharply reduced.

christian-democracy.why: Catholic social teaching, the tradition's base, defends private property (with a social obligation) against collectivisation.
Christian democracy is committed to constitutional multiparty democracy, so it rejects one-party rule.
Its social market economy rests on solidarity, welfare and social partnership, not on market outcomes alone.

catholic-integralism.why: Integralists hold that public law must reflect natural-law teaching that marriage is between a man and a woman, now as well as in the ideal.
Integralism subordinates the temporal power to the spiritual power, as body to soul, which is the opposite of strict separation.
Integralists hold that the state should recognise the true religion, Catholicism.
Integralism denies that law can be neutral and orders it to man's supernatural end as taught by the Church.

islamic-democracy.why: Islamic democracy is defined by elected, accountable government, which permanent single-party rule abolishes.
It holds that the community chooses and can hold its rulers to account, so voters must be able to replace entrenched power.

theocratic-absolutism.why: Theocratic absolutism holds that faith and state are one.
It holds that law is revealed by God, not made from secular reasons, and it rejects liberal secularism now as well.
Theocratic absolutism places lawmaking authority in a supreme religious ruler or clergy.

distributism.why: Distributism's founding claim is that property and wealth must be spread widely, not concentrated in a few hands.
Distributists reject collectivist planning as a route to Belloc's servile state and want production decided by many small proprietors.

gandhian-sarvodaya.why: Gram swaraj builds self-rule from self-governing village republics, so most decisions are made locally rather than nationally.
Gandhian ahimsa rejects relying on overwhelming military force, and the ideal relies on unarmed peace brigades instead.
A pre-emptive military strike breaks non-violence, which Gandhian thought holds even in defence.
Ahimsa governs everything in Sarvodaya, so armed force abroad when no one has attacked is ruled out.
Sarvodaya respects all religions equally and prefers none, which an official religion would contradict.

national-conservatism.why: Letting an international court override national courts subordinates national self-government to a supranational body, which national conservatives define themselves against.
The doctrine holds that the world should be a family of self-governing nations, which a binding world government would abolish.
National conservatism puts loyalty to the independent nation-state first, so placing a global community above one's country rejects its starting premise.
National conservatives hold that the nation controls who may settle in it, so an unrestricted right to settle anywhere contradicts their view of borders and nationhood.

right-populism.why: Right-populism is defined by the claim that the people's will should prevail over experts and unelected elites.
Handing contested questions to an unelected council of the wise is exactly the elite rule populism exists to oppose.
Right-populists demand that sovereignty be reclaimed from supranational institutions, so a binding world government contradicts them.
Border control and reduced immigration are core right-populist demands, which an unrestricted right to settle anywhere would abolish.

civic-nationalism.why: Civic nationalists treat the nation-state as the main home of self-government, which a binding world government would supersede.
Civic nationalism is still nationalism: it holds that citizens owe their primary political loyalty to their national community.

fascism.why: Fascist doctrine calls for a single party and leader ruling permanently, with rival parties abolished as obsolete.
Fascism holds national sovereignty to be absolute and scorns international bodies, so a binding world government contradicts it.
Fascism treats the nation as the supreme object of loyalty, above any individual, class or international community.

kemalism.why: Republicanism is a founding arrow of Kemalism, which replaced the hereditary Ottoman dynasty with a republic.
Kemalism insists on a unitary, centralised republic, so having most law made by regions contradicts its constitutional design.
Laiklik, one of the Six Arrows, requires that law and politics rest on secular reason rather than religious authority.
Kemalism abolished the caliphate and religious courts specifically to remove clergy from law-making.

peronism.why: Political sovereignty and economic independence, two of Peronism's three banners, put the nation's own people first in loyalty.
Peronist social justice and state-directed development require the state to shape production, not leave it to prices and competition alone.

classical-liberalism.why: Private property is a natural right in classical liberalism, so common ownership of nearly all productive assets contradicts it.
Classical liberalism requires government by consent with power limited and checked, which rules out permanent single-party rule.
Classical liberalism holds that markets and voluntary exchange, not planners, should coordinate the economy.

minarchism.why: Minarchism holds property fully private, so common ownership of nearly all productive assets contradicts it.
The minimal state is limited to police, courts and defence, so it cannot redistribute wealth from rich to poor.
Under self-ownership and non-aggression, punishing a person for conduct that harms only themselves is illegitimate force.
A night-watchman state has no role in planning production, which minarchists leave entirely to markets.

georgism.why: Free trade is a core Georgist commitment, set out in George's own 'Protection or Free Trade'.
Georgism wants taxes on trade replaced by a land-value tax, so tariffs favouring local goods contradict it.
Beyond collecting land rent, Georgism leaves the economy to markets and private enterprise, not central planning.

paleolibertarianism.why: Paleolibertarians treat property rights as absolute and private, so common ownership of nearly all productive assets contradicts it.
Decentralisation, states' rights and secession are central to paleolibertarianism, which sees small units as the safeguard of liberty.
Paleolibertarianism rejects global governance and supranational institutions as the extreme form of the centralised state it opposes.

anarcho-communism.why: Anarcho-communism holds that everything belongs to everyone, with production held in common by communes and workers' associations.
Abolishing capital and private ownership of the means of production is a defining anarcho-communist aim.
Anarcho-communists reject any ruling party or 'workers' state' as a new set of rulers.
It replaces markets and money with distribution by need, so letting prices and competition alone decide production contradicts it.

anarcho-syndicalism.why: In the syndicalist ideal, workers' collectives hold the means of production in common.
Anarcho-syndicalism's programme is for workers to take over the means of production and run them through their syndicates.
It seeks to expropriate capital, so wanting productive assets privately owned by investors contradicts it.
Anarcho-syndicalism rejects all parties and the state, so permanent single-party rule contradicts it.

mutualism.why: Mutualism rejects absentee ownership that collects profit without working, which is exactly what passive shareholding is.
Mutualists want authority dissolved into contract and voluntary federation, which rules out single-party rule.
Mutualism is market anarchism: it holds that markets, not planning, should coordinate production.

libertarian-municipalism.why: Libertarian municipalism calls for land and enterprises to be municipalised, owned in common by the community.
The doctrine rejects private ownership of the economy in favour of control by citizen assemblies.
Libertarian municipalism puts policy-making in face-to-face assemblies, which permanent rule by one party would replace.
Bookchin's confederalism gives wider councils only the coordinating powers that municipal assemblies delegate to them.

anarcho-capitalism.why: Common ownership of productive assets is incompatible with the absolute private property anarcho-capitalism rests on.
Anarcho-capitalism holds that all property is private, including every productive asset.
Because taxation is held to be theft, wealth gained through voluntary exchange belongs entirely to the person who earned it.
Anarcho-capitalists hold that free markets should coordinate everything, with no planning authority.

anarcho-primitivism.why: Anarcho-primitivism rejects the state and all rulers, so long-term single-party rule contradicts it.
Anarcho-primitivists explicitly oppose genetic engineering, still more so for enhancement.
Anarcho-primitivism rejects technology as a system and explicitly opposes AI development.
The tradition opposes life extension as part of the technological project it wants dismantled.

absolute-monarchism.why: Under absolute monarchy the ruler is chosen by hereditary succession, not by a popular vote of adults.
A reigning dynasty being replaceable by voters is incompatible with hereditary, unaccountable-to-voters sovereignty.
Absolute monarchism is defined by undivided sovereign power vested in a hereditary monarch.

constitutional-monarchism.why: A monarch above party politics presupposes competing parties in parliament, which permanent single-party rule would abolish.
Constitutional monarchism holds that the monarch reigns but does not rule, with government accountable to parliament, so one leader acting without lawmakers' approval contradicts it.

technocracy.why: Technocracy is defined by giving qualified experts, not voters, control over technical policy decisions.
Technocratic governance is secular and evidence-based, so giving religious leaders a formal law-making role contradicts it.

confucian-meritocracy.why: Confucian meritocracy holds that governing requires virtue and competence, so officials selected by merit rather than popular opinion should decide.

developmental-authoritarianism.why: Developmental authoritarianism has the state guide industrial priorities rather than letting prices and competition alone decide output.
The developmental state is defined by steering investment and credit toward national development goals.
Leaving investment to pure returns is the unguided market allocation that developmental states reject in favour of industrial policy.

neoreaction.why: Neoreaction rejects democracy and wants citizens treated as customers with exit, not as voters who choose the government.
Neoreaction's ideal is a patchwork of many competing small sovereigns, the opposite of a binding world government.

transhumanism.why: Transhumanists favour genetic therapy and morphological freedom, so a blanket ban on heritable editing for any purpose contradicts them.
Overcoming ageing through life extension is a founding goal of transhumanism.
Transhumanism rejects 'natural' limits and treats ageing as a condition medicine should defeat.
Morphological freedom and brain-computer interfaces are core transhumanist aims, so opposing safe brain-computer links for healthy people contradicts them.
